headline: A stormy Pacific pattern held all week, with the wettest, windiest storms now expected into next week.
summary:
From the start, forecasters saw an active stretch with one Pacific storm after another crossing western Washington, and that call never wavered. What changed was the strength and timing of individual storms. Early in the week the focus was a Friday front and a stronger windstorm Saturday night. Confidence in that windstorm grew, and a High Wind Watch went up for the coast. By the weekend, forecasters were adding a slight chance of thunderstorms near the coast and expecting steadier rain midweek. They also started describing an atmospheric river, a long, narrow stream of moist air aimed at the region, which can keep rain going for days.

By midweek the discussions looked past the first storms to a stronger round late in the week. Wind advisories were issued for the coast and north interior, and heavy rain on the Olympics pushed the Skokomish River into flood. A deep dip in the jet stream, the fast band of high-altitude winds, over the Gulf of Alaska is now steering the next storms toward us. Forecasters expect a mild, soggy weekend, a brief break Monday, and another wetter, possibly windy front Tuesday. They are still unsure of the exact wind tracks and the strength of the weekend storms.

turning_points.what: Forecasters grew confident that Saturday night would bring a significant windstorm, and a High Wind Watch covered the coast.
A brief dry spell was expected, but forecasters now described an atmospheric river aimed at the area and flagged a Friday-to-weekend system to watch.
Wind advisories took effect for the coast and northern lowlands, and the late-week outlook shifted to stronger storms, large coastal swells, and possible minor river flooding.
The Skokomish River flood watch became a flood warning, and storm timing was refined: Thursday night, around Sunday, then a Tuesday front after a likely Monday lull.
